RagShortTexts: The Balliol dynasty held immense estates across Durham and Galloway, founding Balliol.

Variants.Content: Balliol power rested on land as much as on royal favor. John de Balliol held Barnard Castle in County Durham, and his Galloway lordships tied the family to Scottish affairs across the border. With Lady Dervorguilla he built estates on both sides of the Anglo-Scottish frontier, and in the 1260s the couple founded Balliol College at Oxford to house poor scholars. The line held a direct claim to the Scottish crown through descent from David, Earl of Huntingdon. That claim would matter after the Maid of Norway died in 1290, when the Great Cause was argued before Edward I. A split inheritance across two kingdoms was the family's constant weakness.

The Comyns backed the Balliols, and their combined lordships gave the family a dense web of castles across Galloway and the border marches. Each fortified keep could hold a garrison, and each garrison could challenge the Bruces in the field. Alliances like this turned a family dispute into a regional war, so the Balliol lords kept their letters and marriage contracts under close watch.
